questions.problem: Find the domain of the vector-valued function $f(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(-t),\,3,\,\sqrt{{t}^{2}+2}⟩.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the domain of $f$, we need the intersection of the domains of the individual components.

- The domain of the 1st component $\operatorname{ln}⁡(-t)$ is $t\in (-\infty ,0).$

- The domain of the 2nd component $3$ is $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

- The domain of the 3rd component $\sqrt{{t}^{2}+2}$ is $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

The intersection is illustrated in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14135210/assets/39266e152f7a52ee6cf56ad872704a110765e22c5d3fcea6f4b4c7565276ee24.png)

Therefore, the domain of the vector-valued function $f(t)$ is $t\in (-\infty ,0).$

questions.problem:
Which of the following are subsets of ${Q}_{0}^{+}$ (the set of non-negative rational numbers)?

I. ${Z}^{-}$ (the set of negative integers)

II. $N$

III. ${Z}_{0}^{+}$ (the set of non-negative integers)
questions.worked_solution:
$A$ is a subset of $B$ if every element of $A$ is an element of $B.$

With that in mind, let's inspect the given choices.

- ${Z}^{-}$ is not a subset of ${Q}_{0}^{+}.$ For example, $-1\in {Z}^{-}$ but $-1\notin {Q}_{0}^{+}.$

- $N$ is a subset of ${Q}^{+}.$ Indeed, every natural number is also a positive rational number.

- ${Z}_{0}^{+}$ is a subset of ${Q}_{0}^{+}.$ Indeed, every positive integer is also a positive rational number. Notice also that  $0$ is in both  ${Z}_{0}^{+}$ and ${Q}_{0}^{+}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III  only".

questions.problem: If $\,\text{Re}(x)=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\text{Im}(x)=[\begin{aligned}e & f \\ g & h\end{aligned}]\,$ are the real and imaginary parts of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-3-9\text{i} & -7+\text{i} \\ -5-2\text{i} & -4\text{i}\end{aligned}]\,$ then what is the value of $bc-ef?$
questions.worked_solution:
For the given matrix $A,$ we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-3-9\text{i} & -7+\text{i} \\ -5-2\text{i} & -4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\ A & =[\begin{aligned}-3-9\text{i} & -7+\text{i} \\ -5-2\text{i} & 0-4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-3 & -7 \\ -5 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(A)}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}-9 & 1 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(A)}.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $b=-7,c=-5,e=-9$ and $f=1.$ Therefore,

$$
bc-ef=(-7)\cdot (-5)-(-9)\cdot 1=44.
$$

Consider the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y)$ where the graph of $f(y)$ is shown above. Which of the following statements are true?

I. $y=-3$ is a node.

II. $y=2$ is a sink.

III. $y=2$ is a source.
questions.worked_solution:
We can classify the equilibrium solutions of an autonomous ODE ${y}^{′}=f(y)$ by examining its phase line.

- An equilibrium solution is a *sink* if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line both point *toward* the equilibrium solution.

- An equilibrium solution is a *source* if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line both point *away* from the equilibrium solution.

- An equilibrium solution is a *node* if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line point in the same direction.

The phase line that corresponds to the given graph is as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14135210/assets/362ffe8871efa8dc597708b039fa766c3603777ba12460e84d9af1fc39800288.png)

Therefore, we have:

- Statement I is true. From the phase line, we see that $y=-3$ is a node.

- Statement II is true, while statement III is false. From the phase line, we see that $y=2$ is a sink.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only".

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=6t-2$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=-1\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s}$, calculate the speed of the particle at the moment $t=3\,\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (6t-2)\text{d}t \\  & =3{t}^{2}-2t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=-1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & =3(1)^{2}-2(1)+C \\ -1 & =3-2+C \\ C & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=3{t}^{2}-2t-2.$

We evaluate the velocity at time $t=3\,\text{s}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =3(3)^{2}-2(3)-2 \\  & =27-6-2 \\  & =19\,\text{m/s}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the speed is equal to $|v(t)|,$ we conclude that the speed of the particle is $19\,\text{m/s}.$

questions.problem: Determine if the vector $u$ lies on the plane $Π:r=sb+tc,$ $t,s\in R$, where  $b=⟨1,-2,-1⟩$, $c=⟨-4,5,-1⟩$, and  $u=⟨1,1,4⟩.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of $s\cdot t$ from the decomposition $u=sb+tc.$
questions.worked_solution:
By definition, $u\in Π$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc & =u \\ s[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s-4t=1 \\ -2s+5t=1 \\ -s-t=4\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 1 \\ -2 & 5 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & -3 & 3 \\ -1 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & -5 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -5 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+5{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s-4t=1 \\ t=-1 \\ 0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
t=-1.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s-4t & =1 \\ s-4(-1) & =1 \\ s+4 & =1 \\ s & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=-3,\,t=-1,$ we conclude that $u$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
u=-3b-c.
$$

Finally, $s\cdot t=(-3)\cdot (-1)=3.$

questions.problem:
Consider the straight line with the parametric equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=2+4t \\ y=-3+5t \\ z=7-6t\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the corresponding vector equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2+4t \\ -3+5t \\ 7-6t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4t \\ 5t \\ -6t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ -6\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

This implies that the given line passes through the point $P(2,-3,7)$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨4,5,-6⟩.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{y-(-3)}{5}=\frac{z-7}{-6}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$
\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{y+3}{5}=\frac{z-7}{-6}.
$$
